summary.en: An anti-colonial war in 1921–1926 between the Berber tribes of the Rif Mountains in northern Morocco and Spain, which received help from France from 1924–1925. Under Abd el-Krim the Riffians defeated the Spanish army at Annual and founded the Republic of the Rif, but superior strength and Spanish poison gas finally decided the war.

text.en: Wikipedia dates the war to 1921–1926, from the first major battles to Abd el-Krim's surrender. Wikidata instead counts from 8 June 1911 to 8 July 1927, and so includes Spain's earlier campaigns in the area and the last fighting after the surrender.

intro.en: By the Treaty of Fez in 1912, Morocco was divided between a French and a Spanish protectorate, and the Rif Mountains in the north fell to Spain. But the sultans had never ruled the Rif, and the Berber tribes there had taken no part in the agreements that gave Spain the area. Spain, which had lost its last colonies in the Americas and Asia in 1898, wanted to build a new empire in Africa, and the Rif had rich iron ore. The mines forced out the local population, who received no share of the profits. In 1921 General Manuel Fernández Silvestre advanced deep into the Rif Mountains with a poorly supplied army of mostly conscripts, spread out in small outposts. Abd el-Krim, a leader in the Aith Ouriaghel tribe and a former official and translator in the Spanish administration in Melilla, warned him not to cross the Amekran river. Silvestre went on regardless, and on 1 June 1921 the Riffian fighters took a new Spanish outpost on Mount Abarrán, east of Annual.

name.en: The Republic of the Rif and the tribes of the Rif

members.en: Abd el-Krim (Muhammad ibn Abd al-Karim al-Khattabi) and M'hamed el-Khattabi, with Riffian Berbers, Jebala, Ghomara and Senhaja. The core was a well-trained standing army of 2,000–7,000 men according to different accounts; the rest were tribal fighters who could seldom stay away from their farms for long. Abd el-Krim could never arm more than about 20,000 men at one time.

Spain, with the Army of Africa, where Moroccan regulares and the newly formed Spanish Legion, the Tercio de Extranjeros (with Francisco Franco as one of its commanders) became the elite units. From September 1923 the dictator Miguel Primo de Rivera led the war. France entered after the Riffian attacks on the French zone in April 1925, with up to 160,000 men under Marshal Philippe Pétain, among them soldiers from Algeria, Senegal and Morocco.

outcome.en: Spain and France won. After the landing at Alhucemas in September 1925 and the French offensive from the south, Abd el-Krim surrendered to the French in May 1926. He was exiled to the island of Réunion in the Indian Ocean and held there until 1947. The Republic of the Rif was dissolved, but a few groups continued fighting until July 1927. The war divided Spain and contributed to Primo de Rivera's coup in 1923. From about 1923–1924 (the sources give different years) the Spanish army used poison gas, including mustard gas, phosgene and chloropicrin, also against civilians, markets and rivers. It was the first extensive use of gas since the First World War. Some historians see the Rif War as a forerunner of decolonisation in North Africa and of the Algerian War thirty years later, others as one of the last colonial wars.

casualties.en: The figures are uncertain and differ. According to the source's compilation, Spain had 43,500–63,000 casualties and France 10,000–18,000, counting dead, wounded, missing, captured and sick. At Annual and during the retreat in 1921 alone, 13,192 Spanish soldiers died according to the figure given to the Spanish parliament. About 8,600 French soldiers died in battle and from disease. Losses on the Riffian side are estimated at about 30,000, of whom 10,000 were killed, while other sources give 40,000–80,000 soldiers and civilians killed. Both sides committed atrocities, among them the massacre of Spanish soldiers who had surrendered at Monte Arruit in 1921 and the Spanish army's reprisals.

caption.en: Press photo by Jean du Taillis (Agence Rol), 1922: Spanish military camp in the eastern Rif (file page, BnF). The photo was taken a year after the war began (1921) and shows a few soldiers in a mountain landscape, not fighting. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 22 July 1921 about 3,000 Riffian fighters under Abd el-Krim attack the Spanish camp at Annual. General Silvestre's retreat turns into a rout, and Silvestre disappears. The Riffians then take over 130 Spanish outposts, and by the end of August Spain has lost all the land it had conquered in the area since 1909. The defeat, which the Spanish call the Disaster of Annual, is regarded as the worst in the history of the modern Spanish army.

text.en: Wikipedia's article on the battle and Wikidata give 22 July–9 August 1921, from the battle to the surrender at Monte Arruit. Wikipedia's article on the war instead says that the army collapsed on 1 July 1921.

caption.en: The Spanish military camp at Annual in early 1921, before the battle. Photographer unknown. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: The Spanish soldiers who fled from Annual defend themselves in the fort of Monte Arruit. After twelve days of siege, without water or supplies, they surrender on 9 August 1921 on a promise of safe conduct. The Riffian fighters do not keep the agreement but kill most of the soldiers, against Abd el-Krim's orders that prisoners were to be treated well. About 400–600, mostly officers, are held hostage for ransom.

text.en: Wikipedia gives different numbers of dead: over 2,000 in the article on the massacre and in the article on the war, but 3,000 in the article on the Battle of Annual. Spanish troops later found the bodies of 2,600 soldiers. Wikidata gives the same place and the siege 29 July–11 August 1921.

summary.en: On 18 September 1921 Abd el-Krim gathers the tribes' delegates for a congress. He condemns both Spanish and French colonialism, and the congress declares the Rif independent, with Abd el-Krim as emir and a national council. The Republic of the Rif had its own constitution and government and sent envoys to London and Paris, but was never recognised by any other state.

text.en: Wikipedia and Wikidata give 18 September 1921. Wikipedia's article on the republic also says that it was formally founded in 1923, and in another place that Abd el-Krim proclaimed the republic in April 1925.

caption.en: Portrait photo of Abd el-Krim, according to the file page "leader of the Moroccan insurgents, president of the Rif Republic", about 1921; photographer unknown, source Poland's Narodowe Archiwum Cyfrowe. It shows the person, not the proclamation itself (1921). Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 8 September 1925 a Spanish-French fleet lands 13,000 Spanish soldiers at Alhucemas Bay, where Abd el-Krim's own tribe lived. The landing, led by Primo de Rivera and General Sanjurjo, is regarded as the first in history with tanks and extensive air support from the sea. It turns the war, while French troops attack from the south.

caption.en: Postcard from September 1925 captioned "La playa de Morro Nuevo en los días del desembarco" (Morro Nuevo beach during the days of the landing); author unknown, source the Spanish Army Training and Doctrine Command (file page). A contemporary image; it shows ships and landing craft at the beach. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: After a year of hard resistance to the Spanish-French superior force, Abd el-Krim surrenders to the French authorities in May 1926. The Republic of the Rif is dissolved, and Abd el-Krim is exiled to Réunion. A few groups in the Rif continue fighting until July 1927.

text.en: Wikipedia's article on the war gives 27 May 1926, and Wikidata gives the same day for the dissolution of the republic. The article on the Republic of the Rif says that he surrendered to Marshal Pétain on 26 May 1926.

summary.en: A series of armed conflicts in Mexico in 1910–1920 that overthrew Porfirio Díaz, gave the country a new constitution and changed the state and the culture. Peasants, miners and many of the country's Indigenous peoples took part. About a million people died, most of them civilians.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 20 November 1910–1 December 1920 and writes that it is not clear-cut when the revolution ended. Wikidata gives 20 November 1910–21 May 1920, the day President Carranza was killed.

intro.en: Porfirio Díaz had ruled Mexico since 1876. Large estates, haciendas, had seized land that peasants and Indigenous villages had held in common, and strikes were put down by force. When the landowner Francisco I. Madero challenged Díaz in the 1910 presidential election he was imprisoned, and in the Plan of San Luis Potosí he called for an uprising on 20 November 1910. Farm labourers, miners and many from the country's Indigenous population joined in, and the federal army could not put down the uprisings.

members.en: Francisco I. Madero (1910–1913). Emiliano Zapata and the Zapatistas in Morelos: peasants from villages, some of them Nahuatl-speaking, who demanded their land back. Pancho Villa and the Division of the North. Venustiano Carranza and Álvaro Obregón with the Constitutionalists, who won in the end. After 1914 Villa and Zapata fought against Carranza.

name.en: The governments and the old army

members.en: Porfirio Díaz's regime and the federal army (until 1911), and Victoriano Huerta's military regime in 1913–1914. The United States was heavily involved and in 1916 sent a punitive expedition into Mexico after Villa's raid on Columbus, New Mexico.

outcome.en: The federal army was dissolved and replaced by a revolutionary army. The 1917 constitution gave universal suffrage for men, rights for workers and the basis for a land reform (Article 27). Zapata was murdered in 1919 and Carranza in 1920. Revolutionary generals ruled Mexico in 1920–1940, and the party they founded in 1929, later the PRI, governed until 2000.

casualties.en: About a million dead, most of them civilians, according to Wikipedia's summary. Robert McCaa (2001) estimates that perhaps 1.5 million died, and nearly 200,000 fled abroad, mainly to the United States. The figures are uncertain and differ greatly between the estimates.

summary.en: On 21 May 1911 Díaz and Madero make peace in Ciudad Juárez. Díaz resigns on 25 May and goes into exile. The treaty promises no social reforms and leaves the old state and army in place, which leads to new unrest in the countryside.

text.en: The date and place come from Wikipedia. Wikidata's entry for the treaty has no date or place.

summary.en: On 28 November 1911 Emiliano Zapata accuses President Madero of betraying the revolution and demands that land, forests and water taken by the haciendas be returned to the villages. A third of the large estates' land is to be distributed to those who have none. The plan becomes the Zapatistas' founding text and influences the land reforms of the 1920s and 1930s.

text.en: The date and place come from Wikipedia. Wikidata's entry for the Plan of Ayala has no date or place.

caption.en: Handwritten text of the Plan of Ayala, written by Emiliano Zapata and Otilio Montaño and signed on 25 November 1911 (World Digital Library). The file page quotes the historian John Womack, who called the plan the "Sacred Scripture" of the Zapatistas. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 9–19 February 1913 generals from Díaz's time fight the government in Mexico City. About 5,500 people are killed. General Victoriano Huerta changes sides and takes power, and on 22 February Madero and Vice President Pino Suárez are murdered. The coup begins the bloodiest phase of the revolution.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 9–19 February 1913. Wikidata gives the same start and 19 February 1913 as the point in time, but the end date is wrongly given as 19 February 1910.

summary.en: On 23 June 1914 Pancho Villa's Division of the North defeats the federal troops defending the silver city of Zacatecas and its railway junction. It is the bloodiest battle in the struggle against Huerta, who resigns on 15 July.

In April 1915 the former allies meet each other. Álvaro Obregón, Carranza's best general, defends himself at Celaya against Pancho Villa's larger army, which attacks with cavalry across open fields and loses thousands of men. The defeat decides the struggle between the Constitutionalists and Villa.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 6–15 April 1915 but also writes that the second battle was fought on 15–16 April. Wikidata gives 6–15 April 1915.

summary.en: On 5 February 1917 a constituent assembly in Querétaro adopts the constitution that Mexico still has today. It gives universal suffrage for men and strengthens the state, and Article 27 lays the basis for a land reform while Article 123 gives workers rights.

text.en: Wikidata gives the same date but no place; the place comes from Wikipedia.

caption.en: The original cover of Mexico's 1917 constitution, photographed in Mexico's national archive (Archivo General de la Nación). Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 10 April 1919 Zapata is lured to a meeting with Jesús Guajardo, an officer in the government army who pretends he wants to change sides, and is shot dead at the hacienda in Chinameca. The murder was ordered by Carranza's government. For many Mexicans, especially peasants and Indigenous peoples, Zapata stands for the struggle for land and rights according to the Plan of Ayala.

caption.en: Portrait of Emiliano Zapata, photographed by Agustín Víctor Casasola in 1914. The photo was taken five years before the event (1919) and does not show his death. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: When Carranza tries to appoint a civilian successor, the generals from Sonora, Obregón, Calles and de la Huerta, rise in revolt with the Plan of Agua Prieta. Carranza flees from Mexico City and is killed in his sleep in Tlaxcalantongo on 21 May 1920. Obregón is elected president in October.

caption.en: Portrait of Venustiano Carranza by Harris & Ewing, printed in The World's Work in 1915 (no later than 1915 according to the file page). The photo dates from five years before his death (1920) and does not show the event. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 17 December 1903 the Wright brothers make the first powered flight, south of Kitty Hawk.

caption.en: Illustration in the style of an Art Deco poster with flat fields of colour and printing screen, not a historical image.

summary.en: A worldwide war in 1914–1918 between the Allies (the Entente) and the Central Powers. It is among the deadliest wars in history: an estimated 15–22 million soldiers and civilians died.

intro.en: The rise of the German Empire had upset the balance of power in Europe, and the great powers competed for colonies, formed alliances and armed themselves. Tensions in the Balkans reached breaking point on 28 June 1914, when the Bosnian Serb student Gavrilo Princip shot Austria-Hungary's heir to the throne, Franz Ferdinand, in Sarajevo. Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia and declared war on 28 July. Russia mobilised to defend Serbia. In early August Germany declared war on Russia and France, and Britain entered the war when Germany invaded Belgium.

members.en: France, Britain with its empire (among others Australia, Canada, India, New Zealand, South Africa and Egypt), Russia (until 1917), Japan, Italy (from 1915) and the United States (from 1917), among others.
Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire (from November 1914) and Bulgaria (from 1915).

outcome.en: The Allies won. Russia left the war with a separate peace in March 1918, and in autumn 1918 Bulgaria, the Ottoman Empire and Austria-Hungary signed armistices. Emperor Wilhelm II abdicated on 9 November, and the war ended with the armistice on 11 November 1918. At the peace conference in Paris in 1919–1920 Germany lost land in the Treaty of Versailles, was disarmed and had to pay large war reparations. The Russian, German, Austro-Hungarian and Ottoman empires collapsed, and new states were formed, among them Poland, Finland, the Baltic states, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia. The League of Nations was founded to preserve peace. The war also contributed to the spread of the Spanish flu in 1918, when large numbers of soldiers were moved in crowded camps and transports.

casualties.en: An estimated 15–22 million dead, of whom 9–11 million were soldiers and 6–13 million civilians, and about 23 million wounded soldiers. The figures are estimates and are given as ranges.

text.en: The League of Nations was formed to preserve peace. The League could not cope with the unrest between the wars, and that failure helped bring about the Second World War in 1939.
Most Germans felt humiliated by the Treaty of Versailles. The article on Germany's responsibility was called the war guilt clause.
Historians have long disagreed about why the war began, why the Allies won and whether the generals were to blame for the great losses.
Nobody knows exactly how many died. The estimates range from 15 to 22 million soldiers and civilians.

caption.en: German reserves on their way into battle along the road to Albert in northern France, according to the label on the back of the photo. The photo was taken at some point during the war. The Library of Congress states no known restrictions on publication.

summary.en: On 28 June 1914 the Bosnian Serb student Gavrilo Princip shoots Austria-Hungary's heir to the throne Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie in Sarajevo. The murder sets off the July Crisis, which a month later leads to war.

caption.en: The shots in Sarajevo as the illustrator Achille Beltrame imagined them on the front page of the Italian newspaper La Domenica del Corriere in July 1914. A contemporary drawing, not an eyewitness image. Cropped. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: In late August 1914 a German army surrounds and crushes almost the whole Russian 2nd Army in East Prussia. The battle is fought near Allenstein but is named after Tannenberg, about thirty kilometres to the west.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 26–30 August 1914. Wikidata gives 23–30 August 1914. The year and place agree, but not the first day.

caption.en: The German general Paul von Hindenburg and other officers on the battlefield of Tannenberg after the victory over the Russians, according to the National Archives of the Netherlands, which dates the photo to 31 August 1914. Cropped. Licence: CC0.

summary.en: In September 1914 French and British troops stop the German advance about forty kilometres from Paris. Germany's plan to defeat France quickly fails, and the Western Front becomes bogged down in trench warfare that lasts four years.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 5–12 September 1914. Wikidata gives 8–12 September 1914. The year and place agree, but not the first day.

caption.en: German ammunition abandoned at the First Battle of the Marne, according to the Bain News Service title of the picture. Bain gave the date 29 October 1914. Cropped. The Library of Congress states no known restrictions on publication.

summary.en: From 27 August to 7 November 1914 Japanese and British forces besiege the German port city of Qingdao in China. It is the war's only major land battle in Asia and the Pacific.

caption.en: “Banzai, banzai, the fall of Tsingtau”: Japanese colour lithograph from 1914 in which Japanese soldiers attack German soldiers at Tsingtao. A contemporary propaganda picture, not an eyewitness image. Cropped. The Library of Congress states no known restrictions on publication.

summary.en: On 3–5 November 1914 a British-Indian force tries to take the port of Tanga in German East Africa, but is beaten back by a smaller German force under Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck. It is the first major battle in the East African campaign.

caption.en: German colonial troops fire on British soldiers fleeing back to their ships at Tanga on 3 November 1914. Drawing by Carl Arriens in the German work Der Krieg 1914–19 in Wort und Bild, published in 1919: a picture from one side, not an eyewitness image. Cropped. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: The Allies try to take control of the straits to Constantinople. The fleet fails in March 1915, and the troops who land on the peninsula in April are withdrawn in January 1916 after about 250,000 killed, wounded and captured on each side. The day of the landing, 25 April, is today Anzac Day in Australia and New Zealand.

text.en: Wikipedia counts the campaign from the fleet's first attack on 19 February 1915 to 9 January 1916. Wikidata counts from the landing on 25 April 1915. The year and place agree, but not the start day.

caption.en: “Turk battery, Gallipoli” (Bain News Service title): an artillery battery on the Gallipoli peninsula. The Library of Congress describes the soldiers as Ottoman and dates the photo from when the campaign took place, 1915–1916. Cropped. The Library of Congress states no known restrictions on publication.

summary.en: From December 1915 Ottoman troops besiege a British-Indian garrison in the town of Kut, south of Baghdad. The garrison surrenders on 29 April 1916, and many of the prisoners die on the march into captivity in Aleppo.

caption.en: General Charles Townshend and the Ottoman commander Khalil Pasha with officers shortly after the garrison of Kut had surrendered, 1916. Cropped. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: From 21 February to 18 December 1916 German troops attack the French fortifications around Verdun. It becomes the longest battle of the war and ends in a French victory.

caption.en: A French soldier in full winter gear, photographed at the Verdun front. From the newspaper The Madison Journal, 30 December 1916. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 31 May–1 June 1916 the British and German fleets meet in the largest naval battle of the war. 14 British and 11 German ships are sunk. Both sides claim victory, but the German fleet afterwards avoids new major naval battles.

caption.en: The British battleships Warspite and Malaya during the Battle of Jutland, photographed from the battleship Valiant on 31 May 1916. Cropped. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: From 1 July to 18 November 1916 British and French armies attack the German lines at the Somme. Over three million soldiers take part, and more than a million are killed or wounded. Tanks are used for the first time in September.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 1 July–18 November 1916. Wikidata gives 1 July–17 November 1916. The year and place agree, but not the last day.

caption.en: British soldiers wait in a support trench at Beaumont-Hamel shortly before the attack on 1 July 1916, and some are still asleep. Cropped. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 6 April 1917 the US Congress declares war on Germany. Germany had resumed unrestricted submarine warfare, and the Zimmermann Telegram, a secret German offer to Mexico, had outraged Americans. American troops begin to arrive in Europe the same year.

caption.en: President Woodrow Wilson asks Congress to declare war on Germany, 2 April 1917. Four days later Congress declared war. Coloured print, cropped. The Library of Congress states no known restrictions on publication.

summary.en: On 3 March 1918 Soviet Russia makes a separate peace with the Central Powers and leaves the war. Russia loses, among other things, Ukraine, Poland, Belarus and the Baltic countries. The peace is annulled by the armistice in November the same year.

caption.en: The peace conference at Brest-Litovsk, according to the Bain News Service caption. The photo is undated, so it does not necessarily show the day the peace was signed. Cropped. The Library of Congress states no known restrictions on publication.

summary.en: The armistice between the Entente and Germany is signed in a railway carriage in the forest at Compiègne and takes effect at 11 o'clock on 11 November 1918. The fighting stops, and the war is over. Peace is made at Versailles on 28 June 1919.

caption.en: Ferdinand Foch (second from right) and the Allied negotiators in front of the railway carriage in the forest of Compiègne after the armistice had been signed, 11 November 1918. Cropped. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: The pandemic lasts from February 1918 to April 1920. About a third of the world's population is infected, and common estimates put the dead at 25–50 million.

text.en: Wikipedia gives February 1918 to April 1920. Wikidata gives January 1918 to December 1920. Where the disease began is unknown. The point is in Kansas, where the earliest probable cases were documented in March 1918, but a 2018 study found evidence against Kansas as the origin, and researchers have also proposed Étaples in France, northern China and Austria.

caption.en: Illustration in the style of an early 20th-century public health poster, not a historical image.

summary.en: The deadliest war in history, between the Allies and the Axis powers. Almost all the world's countries took part, and the fighting spread across Europe, Asia, North Africa and the world's oceans. An estimated 60–75 million people died, most of them civilians.

title.en: About the start and end of the war

text.en: Most historians count the start of the war from Germany's attack on Poland on 1 September 1939. For the war in Asia and the Pacific, other start dates are sometimes given: the beginning of the Second Sino-Japanese War on 7 July 1937, or Japan's invasion of Manchuria on 18 September 1931. The end is not entirely clear either. The war was then often counted as over on 15 August 1945, when Japan accepted the Allies' terms, but the formal surrender was signed on 2 September 1945. The globe follows the most common dates, 1 September 1939–2 September 1945, and Japan's war in China from 1937 is mentioned in the story.

intro.en: The First World War left unresolved conflicts. By the Treaty of Versailles Germany lost land, all its colonies and the right to a large army, and nationalism and a desire for revenge grew in several countries. In Italy the fascists under Benito Mussolini took power in 1922–1925, and in Germany Adolf Hitler became chancellor in 1933. The Nazis abolished democracy and rearmed. The increasingly militaristic Japan invaded Manchuria in 1931, and in July 1937 the conflict with China became a full-scale war. Germany annexed Austria and the Sudetenland. On 23 August 1939 Germany and the Soviet Union signed a non-aggression pact with a secret addition about dividing Poland between them. On 1 September 1939 Germany attacked Poland, and two days later Britain and France declared war on Germany.

members.en: Poland, Britain with the Commonwealth and the empire, France (defeated in 1940), China, the Soviet Union (from the German attack in June 1941; in September 1939 the Soviet Union had itself attacked Poland under the pact with Germany) and the United States (from December 1941). On 1 January 1942 the Soviet Union, China, Britain and the United States, together with 22 smaller or exiled governments, signed the Declaration by United Nations.
Germany, Japan and Italy, united in the Tripartite Pact in September 1940. Hungary, Slovakia and Romania joined in November 1940 and Bulgaria in March 1941. Italy's fascist regime fell in 1943.

outcome.en: The Allies won. Germany surrendered unconditionally on 8 May 1945. After the atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki and the Soviet attack on Manchuria, Japan announced its surrender on 15 August and signed it on 2 September 1945. Germany, Austria, Japan and Korea were occupied, and German and Japanese leaders were put on trial for war crimes. The United Nations was formed, with the victorious powers China, France, the Soviet Union, Britain and the United States as permanent members of the Security Council. The United States and the Soviet Union became rival superpowers, which led to the Cold War, and the decolonisation of Africa and Asia gathered pace.

casualties.en: An estimated 60 to more than 75 million people died, and 67–80 per cent of them were civilians. At least 20 million died of starvation, disease and hardship. The Soviet Union had the most dead (20–28 million), then China (at least 15 million), Germany (6–8.7 million) and Poland (5–6.5 million). Of the 20–25 million soldiers killed, most died on the Eastern Front. In the Holocaust Nazi Germany and its collaborators murdered about six million Jews, roughly two thirds of Europe's Jews. The Nazis also killed millions of Slavs, over 130,000 Roma and other groups, and Japan killed millions of civilians in the areas it occupied. The figures are estimates and are given as ranges.

text.en: The UN was formed to get countries to cooperate and prevent new wars.
The United States and the Soviet Union came out of the war as rival superpowers, and that laid the foundation for the Cold War.
Europe's great powers lost influence after the devastation, and that set decolonisation of Africa in motion.

Most historians count the start of the war from Germany's attack on Poland on 1 September 1939. Others see the Spanish Civil War as the beginning or the prelude. Nor does everyone agree on the end date.
Nobody knows exactly how many died. The estimates range from 60 to 75 million people, and most were civilians.

summary.en: On 1 September 1939 Germany, together with Slovakia, attacks Poland. Among the first fighting is the shelling of Westerplatte at Danzig. Britain and France declare war on Germany on 3 September, and on 17 September the Soviet Union attacks Poland from the east. By 6 October Poland is divided between Germany and the Soviet Union.

caption.en: German motorised troops in a village in Poland during the invasion, September 1939. Photograph by Wittke, German propaganda company. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0 DE.

summary.en: On 10 May 1940 Germany attacks the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg and France. British and French troops are evacuated from Dunkirk, Italy enters the war on 10 June and Paris is taken on 14 June. The armistice is signed at Compiègne on 22 June and takes effect on 25 June 1940. Northern and western France are occupied.

caption.en: The railway carriage in which the 1918 armistice was signed is pulled out of the museum at Compiègne before the armistice negotiations, 21 June 1940. Photographer unknown. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0 DE.

summary.en: British air forces defend Britain against the German air force's attacks in the summer and autumn of 1940. It is the first major campaign fought only by air forces. Germany fails to gain air superiority, and Hitler postpones and finally cancels the planned invasion.

text.en: British sources count the battle from 10 July to 31 October 1940, and that is how it is given here. German historians instead see it as a single campaign from July 1940 to May 1941, including the night bombings known as the Blitz.

caption.en: Spitfires of No. 610 Squadron, Royal Air Force, based at Biggin Hill, flying in formation, 24 July 1940. Photograph by B. J. Daventry, Royal Air Force. Licence: public domain according to Wikimedia Commons.

summary.en: On 22 June 1941 Germany and several of its European allies attack the Soviet Union with more than 3.8 million soldiers. It is the largest military offensive in history and opens the Eastern Front. The operation lasts until 5 December 1941 but does not reach its goals, and the Soviet Union joins the Allies.

caption.en: German soldiers with a gun cross the border into the Soviet Union at border post IV/95 at the start of Operation Barbarossa, June 1941. Photograph by Johannes Hähle. Licence: public domain.

summary.en: On 7 December 1941 Japanese aircraft from six aircraft carriers attack the American Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor. 2,403 Americans are killed. Within a few hours Japan also attacks, among other places, the Philippines, Malaya, Singapore and Hong Kong. The United States declares war on Japan the next day, and Germany then declares war on the United States.

caption.en: The American destroyer USS Shaw explodes in a floating dry dock during the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor, 7 December 1941. U.S. Navy photograph. Licence: public domain.

summary.en: On 4–7 June 1942 the American navy defeats a Japanese fleet near Midway. American codebreakers have learned of the attack in advance. Japan loses four aircraft carriers, and its advance in the Pacific is halted.

caption.en: The aircraft carrier USS Yorktown is hit by a Japanese aerial torpedo during the Battle of Midway, 4 June 1942. Taken from the cruiser USS Pensacola. U.S. Navy photograph. Licence: public domain.

summary.en: On 7 August 1942 Allied troops, mostly American marines, land on Guadalcanal. It becomes the Allies' first major land offensive against Japan, with fighting both on the island and at sea. Japan withdraws its last forces on 9 February 1943.

caption.en: Japanese air attack on American ships off Guadalcanal on 12 November 1942, during the naval battle of Guadalcanal. The smoke in the background comes from a Japanese plane that had just crashed into the cruiser USS San Francisco. Photograph taken from USS President Adams, U.S. Navy (80-G-32366). Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: From 23 October 1942 the British Eighth Army under Bernard Montgomery attacks the German-Italian Panzer Army at El Alamein. After 13 days of fighting the Axis forces have to withdraw from Egypt and Libya. The threat to the Suez Canal and the Middle East is gone.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 23 October–4 November 1942. Wikidata gives 23 October–11 November 1942.

caption.en: British tanks move up to the battle at El Alamein after the infantry had cleared gaps in the enemy minefield, 24 October 1942. Photograph by Sergeant Gladstone, Army Film and Photographic Unit. Licence: public domain according to Wikimedia Commons.

summary.en: Germany and its allies fight the Soviet Union for the city on the Volga. The battle is regarded as the deadliest of the war. In November 1942 the Red Army surrounds the German Sixth Army, and when the fighting ends on 2 February 1943 it has been wiped out. The victory is widely seen as the turning point of the war in Europe.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 17 July 1942–2 February 1943, when the first fighting took place far outside the city. Other historians count from the German offensive against the city on 23 August 1942, and that is the date Wikidata gives. The end date, 2 February 1943, is the same.

caption.en: The fountain “Children’s Round Dance” on the station square in Stalingrad after the battle. Photograph by Sergey Strunnikov, 1943. Licence: public domain.

summary.en: On 6 June 1944 Allied troops, among them American, British and Canadian, are landed from the air and from the sea on five sectors of the Normandy coast. It is the largest seaborne landing in history and the beginning of the liberation of France and Western Europe.

text.en: Wikipedia gives the landing as 6 June 1944. Wikidata's entry for the Normandy landings gives a longer period, 6 June–29 August 1944.

caption.en: American soldiers of the 1st Infantry Division wade ashore from a landing craft at Omaha Beach in Normandy, around 6 June 1944. Photograph by Robert F. Sargent, U.S. Coast Guard. Licence: public domain.

summary.en: On 27 January 1945 Soviet troops liberate Auschwitz, a Nazi concentration and extermination camp. At least 1.1 million people died there, most of them Jews. The camp became a symbol of the Holocaust, in which about six million Jews were murdered, and since 2005 the day has been the International Holocaust Remembrance Day.

caption.en: A pile of spectacles in Auschwitz. The picture archive’s caption calls the pile witnesses to the mass murder and dates the photograph to January–February 1945. Photographer unknown. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0 DE.

summary.en: On 8 May 1945 Germany's supreme military command signs an unconditional surrender in Karlshorst in Berlin, and the war in Europe is over. The day before, Germany had signed a first surrender in Reims, which the Soviet Union did not accept.

text.en: Wikipedia describes the surrender in Karlshorst in Berlin on 8 May 1945. Wikidata's entry mixes it up with the first surrender in Reims in France on 7 May and gives Reims as the place.

caption.en: Field Marshal Wilhelm Keitel signs Germany’s surrender in Berlin, 8 May 1945. Photograph by Lieutenant Moore, U.S. Army. Licence: public domain.

summary.en: On 6 and 9 August 1945 the United States drops atomic bombs on the Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Between 150,000 and 246,000 people are killed, most of them civilians. These are the only times nuclear weapons have been used in war. Between the bombs the Soviet Union declares war on Japan and attacks Manchuria.

caption.en: The mushroom clouds over Hiroshima on 6 August 1945 (left) and over Nagasaki on 9 August 1945 (right), photographed from American aircraft. The bombs killed between 150,000 and 246,000 people, most of them civilians. Photographs by George R. Caron and Charles Levy. Licence: public domain.

summary.en: On 15 August 1945 Emperor Hirohito announces on the radio that Japan accepts the Allies' terms. On 2 September Japan and nine Allied countries sign the surrender aboard USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay. The Second World War is over.

caption.en: Japanese Foreign Minister Mamoru Shigemitsu signs the surrender on board the battleship USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay, 2 September 1945. Photograph by Stephen E. Korpanty, U.S. Army. Licence: public domain.

summary.en: On 26–29 June 1942, after the defeat at Gazala, Rommel's German-Italian Panzer Army pursues the British Eighth Army into Egypt. The Axis forces take the port fortress of Mersa Matruh with about 6,000 prisoners and many supplies, but are too weak to prevent the British from breaking out to the east.

caption.en: Italian Bersaglieri entering Mersa Matruh on 29 June 1942. Photographer unknown. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 11–26 May 1900, early in the Thousand Days' War, the Conservatives fight the Liberal army under General Gabriel Vargas Santos at Palonegro near Bucaramanga. The Conservatives win. After the battle the war escalates and becomes one of the most brutal conflicts in South America in the early 20th century.

text.en: Wikipedia and Wikidata give the same date but no coordinates. The point comes from the Historical Conflict Event Dataset and lies at Bucaramanga, where Wikipedia places the battle.

summary.en: On 25 August 1942 Japanese naval infantry land at Milne Bay to take the Allied airfields there. The Japanese have underestimated the mostly Australian garrison, and after hard fighting and heavy losses they withdraw on 7 September. The battle is often described as the first major battle in the Pacific War where Allied troops decisively defeated Japanese land forces.

caption.en: Australian troops plough through the mud at Milne Bay, New Guinea, shortly after the unsuccessful Japanese invasion attempt, according to the Australian War Memorial caption. Photograph by Frank Bagnall, 1 October 1942. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: From 21 July to 16 November 1942 Japanese troops fight Australian and Papuan forces along the Kokoda Track across the Owen Stanley Range. The Japanese want to reach Port Moresby overland from the north coast and come within sight of the town, but withdraw at the end of September. The Australians pursue them, and the campaign ends in an Allied victory.

caption.en: Men of the Australian 39th Battalion on parade after weeks of fighting in dense jungle during the Kokoda campaign, 6 September 1942. Photograph by Damien Parer, Australian War Memorial (AWM 013289). Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: After a white dingo hunter has been killed, the police officer William George Murray leads punitive expeditions against the Warlpiri, Anmatyerre and Kaytetye during a severe drought. According to Murray's reports 31 people were killed, but documents, remains and Indigenous oral history point to 70–300 dead, and a more recent study estimates 90. It is the last known massacre of Indigenous people that was approved by the authorities.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 15 August–13 September 1928. Wikidata gives August–October 1928.

summary.en: In 1932–1933 Yolngu men kill five Japanese trepang fishermen, two white men and a police officer, according to later Yolngu accounts as revenge for how the men had treated Yolngu women and the elder Wonggu. The Yolngu elder Dhakiyarr Wirrpanda is sentenced to death, but in 1934 the High Court overturns the sentence in the case of Tuckiar v The King, the first case brought by an Aboriginal man to be heard there. The conflict is counted as one of the last on the frontier.

text.en: Wikipedia says that the High Court heard the appeal in Melbourne on 29–30 October 1934, and in another place in the same article that the sentence was overturned in November 1934. Wikidata has no dates for the crisis.

summary.en: During the Great Depression, settlers in Western Australia complain that about 20,000 emus are destroying their wheat. The Minister of Defence sends three soldiers with two machine guns. Between 2 November and 10 December 1932 the army makes two attempts to shoot the emus, but the birds scatter in small, fast groups and the operation becomes expensive and gives poor results. The press dubs it the “Emu War”. The government said no to further military efforts, and bounties and fencing were used instead.

text.en: The figures differ. After the first attempt, 50 to 500 dead emus were estimated. The commander, Major Meredith, finally reported 986 confirmed hits with 9,860 rounds and a further 2,500 wounded birds that died, but the historian Greg Beyer judges that the figures are probably greatly exaggerated.

summary.en: Neutral Moresnet, an area of 3.5 km² around a zinc mine that the neighbouring countries had governed jointly since 1816, goes to Belgium under the Treaty of Versailles. On 10 January 1920 it becomes the municipality of Kelmis.

caption.en: The Vieille Montagne zinc works in Neutral Moresnet, lithograph from 1855. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 17 August 1945 Sukarno reads out Indonesia's declaration of independence at his house in Jakarta. The Netherlands wants to take back its colony, and four years of armed and diplomatic resistance follow, the Indonesian National Revolution. About 100,000 Indonesians are killed, according to the highest estimate 250,000. After the Round Table Conference in The Hague the Netherlands hands over power on 27 December 1949. Only in 2023 did the Netherlands recognise 17 August 1945 as Indonesia's independence day.

caption.en: Sukarno reads out Indonesia's declaration of independence in Jakarta on 17 August 1945. Photo by Frans Mendur. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 12 January 1904 the Herero people under Samuel Maharero rise against German colonial rule, which had taken their land and cattle. The German commander Lothar von Trotha orders that all Herero men are to be executed, but in practice women and children are killed too. About 40,000–80,000 Herero, 80 per cent of the people, and about 10,000 Nama, half of the people, die. Germany recognised in 2015 that it was a genocide.

caption.en: Prisoners from the Herero and Nama peoples in chains during the war against German colonial rule, 1904–1908. According to the file page, the figure at the right edge is probably a German soldier. Photo by an unknown photographer. The file page gives August 1904, but the date is uncertain. Detail. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 26 June 1945, the last day of a conference in San Francisco with delegates from 50 Allied countries, 50 of the 51 original member states sign the UN Charter. The Charter enters into force on 24 October 1945, and the United Nations then exists.

caption.en: The UN Charter in an exhibition at the UN headquarters in New York, on loan from the US National Archives. Contemporary photograph from 2025, not from 1945. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

summary.en: Early on 15 April 1912 the passenger ship Titanic sinks in the North Atlantic after colliding with an iceberg, on its way from Southampton to New York. Of the 2,208 passengers and crew, about 1,500 perish; the estimates vary. The ship had 20 lifeboats with room for 1,178 people.

caption.en: Titanic leaves Southampton on 10 April 1912, five days before the sinking. Photo by F. G. O. Stuart. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 7 November 1917, which was 25 October according to the calendar Russia then used, the Bolsheviks under Vladimir Lenin rise in Petrograd against the Provisional Government. By the following night they have taken the Winter Palace, where the resistance is weak. The revolution leads to the Russian Civil War and to the formation of the Soviet Union.

caption.en: At the Winter Palace in Petrograd after it had been taken, 26 October 1917 by the old calendar (7 November). Photo by Pyotr Novitsky. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: In 1928 Alexander Fleming at St Mary's Hospital in London discovers that a blue-green mould, which has contaminated one of his culture plates, kills bacteria. He publishes his findings in 1929. From 1939 Howard Florey, Ernst Chain and their group in Oxford turn penicillin into a usable medicine, and in 1944 it is mass-produced. Fleming, Florey and Chain receive the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1945.

caption.en: Alexander Fleming in his laboratory at St Mary's Hospital in London during the Second World War, that is more than ten years after the discovery in 1928. Licence: Public domain (British government work).

summary.en: On 24 October 1929, Black Thursday, a major fall in prices begins on the New York Stock Exchange. On Black Monday and Black Tuesday, 28 and 29 October, the Dow Jones index falls by a total of 23 per cent. The crash becomes the start of what develops into the Great Depression across the world.

caption.en: Crowds outside the New York Stock Exchange on Black Thursday, 24 October 1929. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 13–30 July 1930 the first World Cup in football is played in Montevideo in Uruguay, which the same year celebrates a hundred years since the country's first constitution. 13 teams take part. In the final at the Estadio Centenario on 30 July Uruguay beat Argentina 4–2.

caption.en: The Estadio Centenario in Montevideo in 1930. Photo by an unknown photographer. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 12 March 1930 Mahatma Gandhi begins walking from the Sabarmati Ashram to the coastal village of Dandi, a distance of about 385 kilometres, in protest against the British salt monopoly. On 6 April he breaks the salt laws at Dandi. In the campaign that follows, over 60,000 Indians are imprisoned.

caption.en: Mahatma Gandhi during the Salt March in March 1930. Photo by an unknown photographer. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 15 August 1914 the Panama Canal was formally opened, when the cargo ship SS Ancon passed through. The canal is about 82 kilometres long and links the Atlantic with the Pacific across the Isthmus of Panama, so that ships avoid the long and dangerous route around the southern tip of South America. France began the construction in 1881 but gave up in 1889, and the United States took over the work in 1904. About 5,600 workers died of disease and accidents during the American construction period.

caption.en: Photo by Stan Shebs of the Gatun Locks of the Panama Canal (file page: 2 January 2000). Not from the opening of the canal (1914). Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0.

summary.en: The volcano Mont Pelée on Martinique began erupting on 23 April 1902. Just after 8 o'clock in the morning on 8 May a glowing cloud of ash and gas rushed down the mountain and reached the town of Saint-Pierre within minutes. Almost all of the about 28,000 people in the town died. Among the few survivors was a prisoner in a windowless cell.

Frederick Banting and Charles Best isolated insulin at the University of Toronto in 1921. On 11 January 1922 the 14-year-old Leonard Thompson, who lay dying of diabetes at Toronto General Hospital, received the first insulin injection. The extract was too impure, but James Collip improved it, and a new dose on 23 January worked.

caption.en: Frederick G. Banting and Charles H. Best with a dog on the roof of the Medical Building at the University of Toronto, August 1921, photographed by Henry Mahon according to the file page. The image shows the researchers a year before the first insulin treatment of a patient (1922); it does not show the treatment. Licence: CC BY 2.0.

summary.en: On 1 January 1901 Australia's constitution came into force. The six British colonies New South Wales, Queensland, South Australia, Tasmania, Victoria and Western Australia became states in the Commonwealth of Australia. They kept their own parliaments but gained a joint federal government. Fiji and New Zealand took part in the negotiations but chose to stay outside.

caption.en: Parliament House in Hobart, Tasmania, 1901, decorated for the Federation celebrations. Photograph by an unknown photographer, from the National Archives of Australia. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 19 March 1932 the Sydney Harbour Bridge was opened, a steel arch bridge across Sydney Harbour between the city centre and the North Shore. It was designed and built by the British company Dorman Long under the engineer John Bradfield, and it carries trains, cars, bicycles and pedestrians. At 134 metres from top to water it is the world's tallest steel arch bridge. Its shape has given it the nickname “the Coathanger”.

caption.en: Sydney Harbour Bridge. Modern photo (2006). Detail. Licence: CC BY 2.5.

summary.en: After the 1907 Imperial Conference and at the request of the country's parliament, King Edward VII issues a proclamation, dated 9 September 1907, that the colony is to be called the Dominion of New Zealand. On 26 September Prime Minister Joseph Ward reads out the proclamation on the steps of Parliament, and the day becomes Dominion Day. The change was mainly symbolic, and Britain kept control of defence and partly of foreign affairs.

On 10 July 1931 Norway proclaimed the occupation of part of East Greenland, which was called Eirik Raudes Land. Denmark took Norway to the Permanent Court of International Justice in The Hague, which ruled on 5 April 1933 that the occupation was invalid. Denmark thereby gained sovereignty over all of Greenland.

text.en: Lex calls the court Den Internationale Domstol (the International Court). The judgment is in Series A/B No. 53 of the Permanent Court of International Justice (PCIJ), the predecessor of today's International Court of Justice.

summary.en: On 9 April 1941, one year after Germany had occupied Denmark, Denmark's envoy in Washington, Henrik Kauffmann, on his own initiative signed an agreement with the United States “in the name of the King”. The United States was allowed to build airfields and bases in Greenland and take responsibility for the island's defence. The government in occupied Copenhagen dismissed him.
The general election in September 1911 was the first in Sweden with universal male suffrage. Women could not yet vote for the Riksdag; they did so for the first time in 1921.

The Riksdag made the first decision on equal and universal suffrage for women on 24 May 1919 and the second on 26 January 1921, since a constitutional amendment requires two decisions. In the elections of September 1921 women voted for the first time. Four women were elected to the second chamber, Elisabeth Tamm, Nelly Thüring, Agda Östlund and Bertha Wellin, and Kerstin Hesselgren to the first chamber.

On 25 April 1930 the Soviet security service OGPU set up an administration for labour camps, the Gulag. The camps were spread across the Soviet Union and were at their largest from the 1930s to the early 1950s. About 18 million people were held in camps and labour colonies in 1930–1953. Researchers most often estimate that 1.5–1.7 million died there or shortly after release.

text.en: The number of prisoners is given as 14–18 million for 1930–1953, and Orlando Figes estimates 25 million for 1928–1953. Estimates of the number of deaths range from about 1.05 million (an archival study from 1993, for 1934–1953) through 1.6–1.7 million (the most common estimate) to 2.5–2.75 million when more types of camp or deaths shortly after release are included. Golfo Alexopoulos (2018) estimates about 6 million, but other researchers question that figure.

caption.en: Driver's licence issued on 7 January 1941 to a prisoner of the labour camp at Kandalaksha (file page; the text is in Russian). It shows a document about one prisoner, not camp life in general; the person is not named here. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: In 1932–1933 millions of people starved to death in Soviet Ukraine, most of them in the spring of 1933. The famine followed the collectivisation of agriculture, very high grain delivery quotas that were enforced even when people no longer had food, and harsh punishments such as the Law of Spikelets of 1932. Recent research estimates 3.5–5 million dead in Ukraine. Ukraine and 33 other UN member states recognise the Holodomor as genocide. Researchers agree that the famine was mainly man-made, but disagree on whether it was intentional and aimed at Ukrainians.

text.en: Recent research estimates 3.5–5 million dead in Ukraine. A joint statement to the UN by 25 countries in November 2003 gave 7–10 million. Besides Ukraine, people also died in northern Kuban and among Ukrainians in Kazakhstan. Whether the famine was an intentional genocide is disputed among researchers.

summary.en: On 14 April 1909 the physician Carlos Chagas took blood samples from Berenice, a two-year-old girl in Lassance, Brazil. He found a new parasite, which he named Trypanosoma cruzi. Chagas was in Lassance to investigate malaria, which had struck the workers on a new railway. He described a previously unknown infectious disease in detail: the pathogen, the vector, the host, the symptoms and the spread.

On 20 December 1938 the trade union confederation LO and the employers’ confederation SAF sign a main agreement. It sets rules for how the parties negotiate, how disputes are settled, for dismissals and limits on strikes and lockouts that harm society.

text.en: Swedish Wikipedia says both that the agreement was concluded in Saltsjöbaden, where negotiations began in 1936, and that it was signed at Blasieholmen in Stockholm. Wikidata gives no place. The marker is therefore placed in Stockholm, and the location is approximate.

caption.en: Photo by Meyerhöffer, 20 December 1938: the signing of the Saltsjöbaden Agreement (file page; source: Lars Olsson, Klass i rörelse, 2002). The categories on the file page mention the Swedish Trade Union Confederation, August Lindberg and Sigfrid Edström; the image does not say who is sitting where. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 10 December 1901, the fifth anniversary of Alfred Nobel’s death, the first Nobel Prizes were awarded. In his will Nobel had set out five prizes: physics, chemistry, physiology or medicine, literature and peace. The Peace Prize is awarded in Norway, the others in Stockholm. The first prize in physics went to Wilhelm Röntgen for the discovery of X-rays. The economics prize in Nobel’s memory was only created in 1968.

On 24 July 1911 the American historian Hiram Bingham was led up to the Inca ruins of Machu Picchu by the farmer and innkeeper Melchor Arteaga. The site was known locally: on the mountain two Quechua farmers, Richarte and Alvarez, were working the old terraces, and in 1902 Agustín Lizárraga had written his name and the year in charcoal on a window of the Temple of the Three Windows. Bingham first wrote that Lizárraga was the discoverer of Machu Picchu but later played down his role.

On 21 April 1913 the silent film Raja Harishchandra premiered at the Olympia Theatre in Bombay, and on 3 May it opened to the public at a cinema in the Girgaon district. Dadasaheb Phalke directed and produced it, and it is often considered India’s first feature film. No women were available for the parts, so men also played the female roles. The film was a success and laid the foundation for the country’s film industry.

In April 1921 Simon Kimbangu, a catechist in a Baptist mission, began preaching and, according to his followers, healing the sick, and large crowds came to listen. The movement became the beginning of Kimbanguism, one of the large independent African churches. The Belgian colonial authorities saw it as a threat, and in June they tried to arrest him. In September he gave himself up, and he remained in prison until his death in 1951. The church was banned but spread in secret, and in 1959 it was recognised by the Belgian authorities.

text.en: The sources say that Kimbangu was born in Nkamba and that the church has its headquarters there, but not exactly where he preached in 1921. The point stands for the area.

summary.en: On 4 November 1922 excavators led by Howard Carter, with George Herbert, Earl of Carnarvon, as patron, found a first step in the Valley of the Kings. It led to tomb KV62, where the Eighteenth Dynasty pharaoh Tutankhamun had been buried. Robbers had entered twice shortly after the burial, but the mummy and most of the grave goods remained, because the entrance had been covered by debris. The find became the most famous in the history of Egyptology.

caption.en: Modern photo (2016) by EditorfromMars from the tomb of Tutankhamun (KV62) in the Valley of the Kings: an interior wall with paintings and hieroglyphs. The file page only says "Inside Pharaoh Tutankhamun's tomb, 18th dynasty". Not from the discovery in 1922; no remains are visible. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

summary.en: From 1 to 22 July 1944, 730 delegates from the 44 Allied nations met at the Mount Washington Hotel in Bretton Woods. Their task was to arrange the world’s monetary and financial order after the Second World War. Once ratified by the member governments, the agreements signed there established the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (later part of the World Bank) and the International Monetary Fund. The arrangement became known as the Bretton Woods system. The countries wanted to avoid the problems of the interwar years, such as countries leaving the gold standard, the Great Depression and the trade wars.

caption.en: Modern photo (2014) by Barry Livingstone of the Gold Room in the Mount Washington Hotel, where the agreements establishing the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank were signed in 1944, according to the file page. Not from the time of the event. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0.

summary.en: In July 1905 peoples in German East Africa, present-day Tanzania, rose up against German colonial rule. The spirit medium Kinjikitile Ngwale gave his followers a war medicine of water, maji in Swahili, which was to turn German bullets into water. The Germans burned villages and fields and deliberately caused a famine, tactics that scholars have described as genocidal. When the uprising was crushed in August 1907, 75,000–300,000 people had died, most of them from starvation.

caption.en: Modern map with German labels of the area of the Maji Maji rebellion in German East Africa, drawn by Maximilian Dörrbecker after a map in a book from 2017. The boundary of the area is approximate. The map’s title gives July 1905–July 1908, the event’s sources August 1907. Licence: CC BY-SA 2.5.

summary.en: In 1909 the Swedish parliament passed a law on national parks, and nine parks were created that year, among them Sarek and Abisko in Lapland. Sweden thus became the first country in Europe with national parks. The polar explorer Adolf Erik Nordenskiöld had first proposed using the idea of Yellowstone in Sweden, and scientists pressed for the protection of Sarek in particular. In the same year Sweden got its first laws on nature conservation.

On 1 September 1914 Martha, the last known passenger pigeon, died at the Cincinnati Zoo. The passenger pigeon was once the most abundant bird in North America, with around 3 billion and possibly up to 5 billion birds. In the 19th century it was hunted on an enormous scale for its meat, and deforestation destroyed its habitat. According to a plaque in Indiana, the last confirmed wild passenger pigeon was shot in 1902.

text.en: According to a plaque in Indiana, the last confirmed wild passenger pigeon was shot in Laurel in 1902. The same source says the last fully authenticated record of a wild passenger pigeon was near Oakford, Illinois, on 12 March 1901.

summary.en: On 11 June 1926 the South African parliament passed a national parks law, and Kruger National Park became the country's first national park. The area had first been protected in 1898 by the government of the South African Republic, to control hunting and protect the dwindling animal populations. The peoples living in the reserve were removed over the following decades, and in 1969 the government forcibly relocated about 1,500 Makuleke people from the northern part of the park.

caption.en: A rhinoceros in Kruger National Park. Modern photo (2012), not from 1926. Licence: CC BY 2.0.

summary.en: In the 1930s the prairies of North America were hit by severe drought and huge dust storms. Farmers had ploughed up the deep-rooted prairie grasses, and when the drought came the loose soil blew away in clouds that sometimes darkened the sky. The drought came in three waves: 1934, 1936 and 1939–1940. Tens of thousands of poor families left their farms, many of them for California.

text.en: Wikipedia gives the Dust Bowl as lasting from 1930 to 1940, and Wikidata gives 1930 to 1936.

caption.en: Buried machinery in a barn lot in Dallas, South Dakota, on 13 May 1936, during the Dust Bowl. Photo from the US Department of Agriculture. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 7 September 1936 the last known thylacine died at the zoo in Hobart, Tasmania. The thylacine was a carnivorous marsupial, and in Tasmania it was heavily persecuted in the 19th century because it was seen as a threat to sheep. Between 1888 and 1909 the Tasmanian government paid bounties for it. The Tasmanian government protected the species on 10 July 1936, 59 days before the last animal died.

text.en: Wikipedia says the animal died on the evening or night of 7 September 1936, and Wikidata gives 6 September 1936. According to Wikipedia, researchers also disagree about the animal's sex, how it was caught and whether it died of old age or of neglect.

caption.en: Thylacines at the Beaumaris Zoo in Hobart, photo from 1910. Photographer unknown; source: National Archives of Australia. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: In 1945 the Chilean poet Gabriela Mistral received the Nobel Prize in Literature, the first author from Latin America to do so. Her real name was Lucila Godoy Alcayaga; she was born in Vicuña and grew up in the Andean village of Montegrande. She was also a teacher, journalist and diplomat. Her poems deal with nature, love, sorrow and Latin American identity, among other themes.

In 1905 Albert Einstein published four papers in the German journal Annalen der Physik. They dealt with the photoelectric effect, Brownian motion, the special theory of relativity and the relation between mass and energy, E = mc². The work on the photoelectric effect later earned him the Nobel Prize in Physics.

On 6 January 1912 the German meteorologist and polar researcher Alfred Wegener put forward the idea that the continents slowly move, in a lecture at the Senckenberg Museum in Frankfurt am Main. He argued that they had once been joined in a single landmass, which he called Pangaea. Many geologists rejected the idea, because no one could explain what would drive the movement.

caption.en: Photo from the Danish Expedition to Queen Louise Land and the overwintering in Greenland, 1912/13, taken by Alfred Wegener (file page; archive of the Alfred Wegener Institute). It shows the expedition, not the theory of continental drift that he presented in 1912. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: In 1924 workers at a limestone quarry in Taung, South Africa, found the fossilised skull of a small child. The anatomist Raymond Dart described it in the journal Nature in February 1925 as a new species, Australopithecus africanus. The Taung Child was one of the first finds of early human relatives in Africa and the first evidence that humanity originated there. Dart's conclusions were at first sharply criticised.

caption.en: Object: a replica of the Taung Child’s skull, photographed in 2019 at the Musée des Civilisations Noires in Dakar, Senegal. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

summary.en: In 1924 the physicist Satyendra Nath Bose at the University of Dhaka wrote a paper deriving Planck's radiation law in a new way, by counting the states of particles that cannot be told apart. A journal turned the paper down, and Bose sent it to Albert Einstein, who translated it into German and had it published the same year. Einstein extended the idea to atoms in 1924–1925, and it is now called Bose–Einstein statistics.

On 28 February 1928 the physicist C. V. Raman and his student K. S. Krishnan in Calcutta obtained spectra showing a new kind of light scattering: a small part of the light passing through a transparent substance changes wavelength. Raman announced the discovery to the press the same day, and the phenomenon is called the Raman effect. Raman received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1930, and the day is celebrated in India as National Science Day.

In 1929 the astronomer Edwin Hubble published that the galaxies are moving away from Earth, and that those farther away are moving faster. He built on his own distance measurements at Mount Wilson Observatory, which then had the world's most powerful telescope, and on earlier work by Vesto Slipher and Henrietta Swan Leavitt. The relation is regarded as the first observational evidence that the universe is expanding.

text.en: Alexander Friedmann had already shown in 1922, using the equations of general relativity, that the universe might expand, and Georges Lemaître published the relation between distance and velocity in 1927, two years before Hubble. In 2018 the International Astronomical Union recommended that the law be called the Hubble–Lemaître law.

summary.en: In 1935 the physicist Hideki Yukawa at Osaka University published a new theory of the force that holds protons and neutrons together in the atomic nucleus. The theory predicted a new particle, the meson. When the predicted particle, the pion, was found in 1947, Yukawa received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1949.

caption.en: Hideki Yukawa, photo from the Nobel Foundation archive, 1949 (the year he received the Nobel Prize in Physics). A portrait of him 14 years after he predicted the meson (1935); not from the time of the event. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 19 December 1938 the chemist Otto Hahn in Berlin wrote that he and Fritz Strassmann had obtained barium when they bombarded uranium with neutrons. The physicist Lise Meitner, who had fled to Sweden that year, and her nephew Otto Robert Frisch explained in January 1939 that the uranium nucleus had split, and Frisch called the process fission. Shortly afterwards Hahn and Strassmann predicted that fission releases new neutrons, which made a chain reaction possible.

caption.en: Modern photo (2006) by J Brew at the Deutsches Museum: the apparatus with which, according to the file page, Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann discovered nuclear fission in 1938. The file page's category calls the setup a "mockup" of the experiment, so it may be a reconstruction; not from the discovery itself. Licence: CC BY-SA 2.0.

summary.en: On 2 December 1942 a team led by Enrico Fermi started the first self-sustaining chain reaction created by humans, in the Chicago Pile-1 reactor under the stands of Stagg Field at the University of Chicago. The experiment was secret and part of the Manhattan Project, the Allied effort to build nuclear weapons during the Second World War.

caption.en: Drawing of the first nuclear reactor, erected in 1942 under the stands at Stagg Field at the University of Chicago, by Melvin A. Miller, Argonne National Laboratory; the file page gives no date. According to the file page the reactor consisted of uranium and uranium oxide in a graphite lattice. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: Through an amendment to the constitution on 5 June 1915, women gain the right to vote for both chambers of the Rigsdag, the Folketing and the Landsting. The same day around 20,000 women march in a procession through Copenhagen to Amalienborg. The first election in which women can vote is held in 1918.

In 1932 the carpenter Ole Kirk Christiansen begins making wooden toys in his workshop in Billund. The name LEGO, from the Danish “leg godt” (play well), is introduced in 1934. In time the company becomes a global toy maker.

text.en: Lex spells the founder’s name Ole Kirk Kristiansen, English Wikipedia Ole Kirk Christiansen.

summary.en: On the night of 1–2 October 1943 the German occupiers try to seize the Danish Jews in order to deport them. Most have been warned and have gone into hiding. With the help of the resistance and many Danes, more than 7,000 are taken by boat from the coasts of Zealand to neutral Sweden. A few hundred are caught and taken to Theresienstadt.

text.en: Lex states that more than 7,000 were rescued and that 481 were taken to Theresienstadt. English Wikipedia gives 7,500 rescued and 464 deported to Theresienstadt.

caption.en: Modern photo (2023) by Brigade Piron of a Danish rescue boat in the collection of the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum. According to the file page it was used in the earliest evacuations of Danish Jews, organised by the Helsingør Sewing Club (the "Kiær Line"), carrying 12 to 14 refugees per trip to neutral Sweden. A museum object, not a photo from 1943. Licence: CC BY 3.0.

summary.en: During the First World War the Armenian people and their identity in the Ottoman Empire were systematically destroyed. On the orders of Talaat Pasha, an estimated 800,000–1.2 million Armenians were sent on death marches from Anatolia to the Syrian desert in 1915 and 1916. Estimates of the number of dead range from 600,000 to 1.5 million. Almost all historians outside Turkey regard it as a genocide, and 36 countries have recognised it (2026). The Turkish government maintains that the deportations were a legitimate measure that cannot be called genocide.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 1915–1917 and writes that Turkish nationalists continued massacres and ethnic cleansing of survivors during the Turkish War of Independence. Wikidata gives 24 April 1915 to 1923. Wikipedia gives 600,000–1.5 million dead, and about one million in its introduction; Wikidata gives 1.2 million (700,000–1.7 million).

summary.en: On 15 May 1919 Greek troops landed in Smyrna (İzmir) with Allied backing, which is counted as the start of the war. The Turkish National Movement under Mustafa Kemal, later called Atatürk, set up its own government in Ankara. With the Treaty of Lausanne on 24 July 1923 the government in Ankara was recognised, and on 29 October 1923 the Republic of Turkey was proclaimed. According to the source 13,000 Turkish and 19,362 Greek soldiers were killed; many Greek and Armenian civilians were also killed.

text.en: Wikipedia dates the war to 15 May 1919–24 July 1923 in its introduction, but to 15 May 1919–11 October 1922 in its infobox. Wikidata gives 19 May 1919 as the start, the day Mustafa Kemal landed at Samsun. The infobox also gives about 264,000 Greek civilians killed (according to the political scientist Rudolph Rummel) and 60,000–250,000 Armenian civilians killed.

summary.en: In 1909 a small area on Sonfjället becomes one of Europe’s first national parks. The fell was chosen for its lichen-rich heaths and to protect the last remnant of wild reindeer then left in Sweden. The park was enlarged in 1989 from 27 to 104 square kilometres, and the area has one of Sweden’s densest bear populations.

text.en: Swedish Wikipedia and Wikidata give 1909 (Wikidata 24 May), Lex 1910.

summary.en: Russia and Japan fought over influence in Manchuria and Korea. On the night of 8 to 9 February 1904 Japanese destroyers attacked the Russian fleet at Port Arthur without warning. The victory made Japan a great power, and the defeat contributed to the unrest in Russia in 1905. According to the source between 43,300 and 71,453 died on the Russian side and between 80,378 and 86,100 on the Japanese side.

text.en: Wikipedia and Wikidata give 8 February 1904–5 September 1905. The attack on Port Arthur was made on the night of 8 to 9 February, with the first torpedo attack at about 00:28 on 9 February, and continued the next morning, and Wikipedia’s introduction dates it to 9 February (27 January in the Julian calendar, Old Style). The peace of Portsmouth is dated 5 September (23 August in the Julian calendar).

summary.en: On 10 October 1911 soldiers of the New Army rose in revolt in Wuchang. A provisional government was formed in Nanjing, and on 1 January 1912 the Republic of China was proclaimed with Sun Yat-sen as president. After negotiations with Yuan Shikai, the six-year-old emperor Puyi abdicated on 12 February 1912. This ended the 267-year rule of the Qing dynasty, and with it more than two millennia of imperial rule in China.

caption.en: The revolutionary army storms Nanjing: Chinese colour woodblock print made between 1911 and 1915. The Library of Congress describes it as a battle during the Nanjing uprising of 24 November–2 December 1911. A contemporary popular print, not an eyewitness image. Cropped. The Library of Congress states no known restrictions on publication.

summary.en: The war between the Republic of China and the Empire of Japan began on 7 July 1937 with the incident at the Marco Polo Bridge near Beijing and became a full-scale Japanese invasion. Japan took Shanghai and the capital Nanjing in 1937 and Wuhan in 1938, and the Chinese government moved to Chongqing. Japan formally surrendered on 2 September 1945. According to the source about 20 million people died, most of them Chinese civilians.

text.en: Wikipedia counts the war from 7 July 1937 to Japan’s formal surrender on 2 September 1945. The surrender in China was signed in Nanjing on 9 September 1945, which is the end date in Wikidata and in another part of Wikipedia. The war is sometimes counted from Japan’s invasion of Manchuria on 18 September 1931, and since 2017 this has been China’s official view. The war is often regarded as the beginning of the Second World War in Asia, and Wikidata counts it as part of the Second World War. The number of dead is uncertain: Wikipedia’s infobox gives 14–22 million dead, of whom more than 12 million civilians, and between 455,700 and 700,000 dead Japanese soldiers.

summary.en: On 13 December 1937 the Japanese army took Nanjing, the capital of the Republic of China. In the following weeks Japanese soldiers murdered civilians and prisoners of war, raped women and girls and burned a third of the city. A committee of Westerners, among them the German John Rabe, set up a safety zone that according to the source saved at least 200,000 lives. How many were killed is disputed; newer estimates are between 100,000 and 200,000.

text.en: The International Military Tribunal for the Far East (the Tokyo Tribunal) estimated that more than 200,000 were killed. Other estimates range from 40,000, counting only the city itself, to more than 340,000, counting the whole area between Shanghai and Nanjing. Wikidata gives 300,000 dead. Estimates of the number of rapes range from 4,000 to more than 80,000. According to traditional historiography the massacre lasted six weeks from 13 December 1937. Wikipedia says that the atrocities in the area began on 4 December 1937 and continued until 28 March 1938, and Wikidata gives 13 December 1937–2 February 1938. Japanese nationalists and historical revisionists have denied or minimised the massacre.

summary.en: On 28 June 1919, exactly five years after the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, the peace treaty was signed in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles. Germany had to disarm, give up territory and pay reparations to the Entente powers. The country lost 65,000 km² and 7 million people. In Article 231, the so-called war guilt clause, Germany accepted that Germany and her allies were responsible for the loss and damage of the war.

caption.en: William Orpen's painting "The Signing of Peace in the Hall of Mirrors, Versailles, 28th June 1919" (oil, dated 1919; Imperial War Museums, via Google Art Project). Made the same year as the signing (1919); a commission for the war museum, according to the file page. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: The war began after a partly failed military coup against the left-wing Popular Front government. The uprising started in Spanish Morocco on 17 July 1936 and spread to the garrisons on the mainland the next day. On 1 April 1939 Franco declared victory, and his regime lasted until 1975. Estimates of the number of dead vary widely, from 250,000 to 1 million.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 17 July 1936–1 April 1939, and Wikidata gives 18 July 1936 as the start, the day the uprising reached the mainland. The source says that estimates of the number of dead differ widely: the section on the death toll gives 250,000 to 1 million, and the infobox has several other estimates.

caption.en: Photo from December 1937: Republican soldiers in the streets of Teruel during the capture of the city (file page; Poland's Narodowe Archiwum Cyfrowe). It shows one episode of the war, not the whole war (from 1936). Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: During the Second World War, Bengal in British India was struck by famine. An estimated 800,000 to 3.8 million people died of starvation, malaria and other diseases. Wartime inflation, the loss of rice imports from Japanese-occupied Burma, British wartime measures, trade barriers between provinces and a cyclone with flooding and rice crop disease all contributed, but how much each cause mattered is debated.

In the midst of the war between China and Japan, Henan Province was struck by famine in 1942–1943. The spring and summer rains failed in 1942 and locusts damaged the harvest, in a province where the flooding of the Yellow River in 1938 had already wrecked farming. Both Chinese and Japanese authorities kept requisitioning grain for their soldiers. The death toll is disputed: the researcher Anthony Garnaut estimates around 700,000, while Lloyd Eastman estimated two to three million.

In the night before 27 December 1939 an earthquake of magnitude 7.8 shook Erzincan Province in eastern Turkey. The ground ruptured along about 360 km of the North Anatolian Fault, and the quake caused a tsunami of 1–3 m on the Black Sea coast. 32,968 people died, making it the deadliest natural disaster in Turkey in the 20th century.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 1:57 a.m. on 27 December 1939 local time, and Wikidata gives 26 December 1939.

summary.en: On 23 March 1940 the All-India Muslim League, meeting in Lahore, adopted a resolution calling for "independent states" in the parts of British India where Muslims were in the majority, in the north-west and the east. Later called the Pakistan Resolution, it became the foundation of the Pakistan Movement, and after it the name Pakistan came into wide use.

On 1 June 1945 the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR) was founded with money from one of the Tata family trusts, after the physicist Homi J. Bhabha had asked for support for a research institute. The institute began on the campus of the Indian Institute of Science in Bangalore and moved to Bombay the same year.
