In 1949 TIFR was designated the centre for India’s large-scale nuclear research projects.

caption.en: Modern photo (2007) by Annytifr of a building with a lawn; the file page calls it "tifr picture" and the file name is "Tifr main". Not from the founding (1945). Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 2 September 1945 Ho Chi Minh read a declaration of independence in Ba Đình Square in Hanoi and proclaimed the Democratic Republic of Vietnam. Japan had taken power from the French colonial authorities in March 1945, and after Japan’s defeat the Viet Minh took over in the August Revolution. Emperor Bảo Đại had abdicated on 25 August. No other country recognised the declaration in the following five years.

caption.en: Three sheets of a document in National Archives Centre III (Phông Phủ Thủ tướng, hồ sơ 586, sheets 1–3), with the file title "Bản Tuyên ngôn độc lập của nước Việt Nam Dân chủ Cộng hòa" (Declaration of Independence of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam). The file page description only says it relates to the August Revolution; the sheets are stamped "BẢN SAO" (copy). Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 7 August 1941 the Bengali poet, composer and artist Rabindranath Tagore died, aged 80, in the house in Calcutta where he had been born. In 1913 he had become the first non-European to win the Nobel Prize in Literature. Two of his songs later became national anthems, India’s "Jana Gana Mana" and Bangladesh’s "Amar Sonar Bangla".

caption.en: Rabindranath Tagore in Kolkata; according to the file page probably taken in 1909 and printed in Les Prix Nobel 1913 (1914). A portrait of him alive, not from his death in 1941. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 22 March 1945 the Arab League was founded in Cairo by seven states: Egypt, Iraq, Transjordan, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia, Syria and North Yemen. Its aim was to bring the member states closer together, coordinate their politics, culture and economy and safeguard their independence. The League’s headquarters were in Cairo. Today it has 22 members.

caption.en: The Arab League headquarters in Cairo. Modern photo (2008), not from 1945. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: From 30 January to 8 February 1944 Free French leaders and senior colonial officials met in Brazzaville to discuss the future of the colonial empire. Among other things the conference proposed ending forced labour, removing the special laws that applied only to the indigenous population and setting up elected assemblies in the colonies. Independence and self-government, however, were explicitly rejected.

In March 1944 the ANC Youth League held its first conference, attended by about 200 people. Young activists, among them Anton Lembede, Walter Sisulu, Oliver Tambo and Nelson Mandela, felt that the older generation’s deputations to the government had won Black South Africans no rights. The Youth League brought forward a new generation of leaders, and by the end of the 1940s it had gained control of the ANC.

On 2 August 1942 a royal decree established King Farouk I University in Alexandria, with faculties of arts, law, medicine, science, engineering, agriculture and commerce. It had begun in 1938 as a branch of the university in Cairo. After the revolution of 1952 it was renamed Alexandria University.

caption.en: The main building of Alexandria University. Modern photo (2012), not from 1942. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0.

summary.en: On 21 December 1945 the Ethiopian government founded the wholly state-owned airline Ethiopian Air Lines, with help from an agreement with the American airline TWA. Five Douglas C-47s were bought and flown to Addis Ababa in February 1946, and the first scheduled flight went on 8 April 1946 on the Addis Ababa–Asmara–Cairo route. The company is now called Ethiopian Airlines.

On 13 January 1939, after several years of drought and a heatwave in which Melbourne reached 45.6 °C, large parts of the state of Victoria burned. The fires swept across almost two million hectares, 71 people died and several towns were wiped out. More than 1,300 homes burned down. A Royal Commission afterwards led to major changes in forest management.

On 9 October 1942 an Australian act adopting the Statute of Westminster of 1931 received Royal Assent. From then on the British Parliament could no longer legislate for Australia without the request and consent of the Australian Parliament. The act applied retroactively from 3 September 1939, the day Australia entered the Second World War.

After several weeks of volcanic tremors, Mount Ruapehu on New Zealand’s North Island began erupting in March 1945; the first sign was seen on 8 March. A lava dome grew in the crater lake, which had been emptied of water by July. The eruptions increased from August to November and had ended by January. A dam of ash that formed at the lake’s outlet collapsed in 1953 and caused the Tangiwai disaster.

caption.en: Modern photo (2009) of the Ruapehu volcano massif in Tongariro National Park, by W. Bulach, not from the time of the event. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

summary.en: From 8 November 1939 to 4 May 1940 a large exhibition was held at Rongotai in Wellington to celebrate a hundred years since the Treaty of Waitangi of 1840 and the European settlement that followed. The buildings were designed in Art Deco style, with a 47-metre tower at the centre. Australia, Canada, Fiji and other Pacific islands had their own pavilions or displays. About 2.6 million visitors came.

caption.en: Aerial view of Rongotai, Wellington, 1939, including buildings for the New Zealand Centennial Exhibition. Photograph by William Hall Raine, Alexander Turnbull Library (National Library of New Zealand). Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: Late in the evening of 24 January 1939 an earthquake of magnitude 8.3 struck south-central Chile. More than half of the city of Chillán was destroyed, and in Concepción almost all houses collapsed. Around 28,000 people died, making it the deadliest earthquake in Chile’s history, with more deaths than the great Valdivia earthquake of 1960.

caption.en: Memorial plaque next to the cathedral in Chillán, Chile, commemorating the roughly 30,000 people who died in the 1939 earthquake, according to the file page. Modern photo (2010) by Walter Mooney, U.S. Geological Survey; not from the time of the event. Licence: CC BY 2.0.

summary.en: On 15 January 1944 an earthquake destroyed much of the city of San Juan in western Argentina. About 10,000 people died, a tenth of the city’s inhabitants, and a third of the province’s population became homeless. During the fundraising for the victims, Colonel Juan Perón met his future wife Eva Duarte, and the rebuilding gave the city new building rules for earthquakes.

caption.en: The government house (Casa de Gobierno) of San Juan Province in Argentina, completely destroyed by the 1944 earthquake, according to the file page. A photo from 1944, reproduced from Ursulina Cantoni's book about Federico Cantoni. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 1 May 1943 Brazil’s consolidated labour code, the Consolidação das Leis do Trabalho (CLT), was adopted, issued as a decree by President Getúlio Vargas. The constitution allowed him to make laws by decree while parliament did not meet, and it never met while that constitution was in force. The CLT still governs relations between employers and employees in Brazil.

In 1930 an African malaria mosquito, then called Anopheles gambiae (DNA later showed it to be Anopheles arabiensis), was found in Brazil. It spread malaria very efficiently, and in 1938 it caused the greatest malaria epidemic ever seen in the Americas. By 1940 the mosquito had been completely eradicated from northeast Brazil, by spreading the arsenic compound Paris green where the larvae grew and spraying pyrethrum where the adults rested.

text.en: The article on the history of malaria says the mosquito was discovered in 1930, caused a major epidemic in 1938 and was eradicated in 1940. The article on Anopheles arabiensis instead says it was a brief invasion of Brazil in 1930 that was quickly eradicated.

caption.en: Modern photo (1994) by CDC/James D. Gathany of an Anopheles gambiae mosquito that has landed on the skin and begun to take a blood meal; the file page states that A. gambiae is a known malaria vector. The image shows the species, not the eradication in Brazil. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: The parliamentary reform of 1906 replaces the Diet of four Estates with a single-chamber parliament elected by universal and equal suffrage. Women can both vote and stand for election on the same terms as men. In the first election in 1907, 19 women are elected.

The chairman of the Senate, P. E. Svinhufvud, reads a declaration of independence to Parliament in Helsinki on 4 December 1917, and Parliament adopts it on 6 December. The government of Soviet Russia recognises Finland’s independence by a decree on 31 December 1917.

On 7 June 1905 the Storting declares the union with Sweden dissolved. In a referendum on 13 August almost everyone votes for the dissolution, and on 26 October Oscar II renounces the Norwegian throne. In November the Storting elects the Danish Prince Carl as king, Haakon VII.

text.en: The sources differ on the number of yes votes on 13 August: 368,392 according to Store norske leksikon and 368,208 according to English Wikipedia. Both give 184 no votes. In Sweden, 26 October counts as the day of the dissolution.

summary.en: On 11 June 1913 the Storting decides unanimously and without debate that women shall have universal suffrage in elections to the Storting. Women had gained limited suffrage in Storting elections in 1907 and universal suffrage in local elections in 1910. The first Storting election after the decision is held in 1915.

On 1 December 1918 Iceland and Denmark sign the Act of Union. Iceland is recognised as a fully independent and sovereign state, the Kingdom of Iceland, with the same king as Denmark. Denmark handles foreign affairs and defence at Iceland’s request, and the act is to be revised in 1940.

On 17 June 1944 the Republic of Iceland is proclaimed at a session of the Althing at Þingvellir. In a referendum in May, 97.4 per cent of voters had backed the Althing’s decision to end the union with Denmark, and 95 per cent wanted a republic.

The Salvation Committee, the executive body of the Provincial Assembly (Maapäev), proclaims the Republic of Estonia. The manifesto is read out in Pärnu on the evening of 23 February and distributed in Tallinn on 24 February, today Estonia’s national day. Germany does not recognise the republic and hands over power only in November 1918.

Estonia and Soviet Russia make peace in Tartu, ending the Estonian War of Independence of 1918–1920. Soviet Russia unreservedly recognises Estonia’s independence, the first de jure recognition, and the border between the two countries is drawn. The treaty is often called Estonia’s birth certificate.

Estonia receives a Soviet ultimatum on 16 June 1940, and the Red Army occupies the country. After a rigged vote in an assembly, Estonia is incorporated into the Soviet Union on 6 August 1940. Most Western countries never recognised the annexation and regarded it as illegal.

text.en: Store norske leksikon gives the ultimatum on 16 June, the occupation on 17 June and the annexation on 6 August 1940. Wikipedia gives the ultimatum on 16 June and the incorporation on 6 August, but no separate date for the entry of the troops.

summary.en: On 14 June 1941 the Soviet NKVD begins deporting people from Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. Several thousand people are taken from Estonia to prison camps and forced settlements in Siberia and Central Asia. The men were usually imprisoned, and most of them died in the Gulag.

text.en: According to the official NKVD reports cited by Wikipedia, 5,978 people from Estonia were sent to forced settlements. Another estimate in the same article is 10,000–11,000 sent to prison camps and forced settlements, and Store norske leksikon writes that over 10,000 were deported.

summary.en: On 18 November 1918 the People’s Council of Latvia proclaims the country’s independence from the stage of what is today the National Theatre in Riga. Jānis Čakste leads the council and Kārlis Ulmanis heads the provisional government. After fighting Bolshevik and German forces, Latvia is recognised by Soviet Russia in 1920.

After a Soviet ultimatum on 16 June 1940, Soviet troops enter Latvia the next day. In July an election is held with only one permitted list, and on 5 August 1940 Latvia becomes a Soviet republic. Apart from Germany, no Western country recognised the annexation as lawful.

On 30 November and 8 December 1941 the German Einsatzgruppe A, helped by the Latvian Arājs Kommando, shoots about 25,000 Jews in the Rumbula forest: about 24,000 from the Riga ghetto and 1,000 from Germany. During the German occupation about 90 per cent of Latvia’s Jews were murdered.

On 16 February 1918 the Council of Lithuania, 20 members chaired by Jonas Basanavičius, signs an act in Vilnius restoring an independent, democratic Lithuanian state. The country is then held by Germany, which bans publication of the act. The original was found in an archive in Berlin in 2017.

In January 1923 a revolt staged by Lithuania takes power in the Klaipėda Region, which the Treaty of Versailles had detached from Germany and which was under French administration. In 1925, 43.5 per cent gave German as their language. The 1924 convention makes the region autonomous within Lithuania, and in March 1939 Nazi Germany takes it.

After a Soviet ultimatum the Red Army enters Lithuania on 15 June 1940. In July an election is held in which only the Communists and their allies may stand, and in early August Lithuania is admitted to the Soviet Union. The annexation was not widely recognised abroad.

text.en: Wikipedia dates the ultimatum to 14 June 1940 and Store norske leksikon to 15 June. Store norske leksikon gives 3 August for the annexation, Wikipedia early August.

summary.en: From July 1941 to August 1944 German SS and SD units and the Lithuanian Ypatingasis būrys shoot up to 100,000 people at Paneriai outside Vilnius, most of them Jews but also Poles and Soviet prisoners. About 90 per cent of Lithuania’s Jews were murdered during the occupation.

text.en: Wikipedia gives up to 100,000 dead, about 70,000 of them Jews; the Soviet exhumation after the war gave 70,000–100,000. Monika Tomkiewicz (2008) gives 80,000, of whom 72,000 were Jews. For the Poles, both 1,000–2,000 and about 20,000 are given.

summary.en: The electoral reform of 1918 gives the parliamentary vote to all men over 21 and to women over 30 who meet a property qualification, in Great Britain and Ireland. The male electorate grows to 12.9 million and the female is 8.5 million. Women gained the vote on equal terms with men only in 1928.

On 3 May 1921 the Government of Ireland Act takes effect and divides Ireland into two self-governing parts within the United Kingdom: Northern Ireland, six of Ulster’s counties, and Southern Ireland. Unionists win the election in the north, and its parliament first meets on 7 June. Partition was accompanied by violence in 1920–1922.

On Easter Monday, Irish republicans seize key buildings in Dublin and proclaim an Irish Republic from the General Post Office. After six days they surrender. At least 485 people die, more than half of them civilians, and 16 rebels are executed. The executions increased support for independence.

Under the Anglo-Irish Treaty, 26 of Ireland’s 32 counties become the Irish Free State, a Dominion of the British Empire; the six counties of Northern Ireland stay outside. A civil war over the treaty lasts until May 1923. In 1931 the state gains internationally recognised independence, and in 1937 it takes the name Ireland.

On 16–17 July 1942 French police, at the request of the German occupiers, arrest 13,152 Jews in Paris, among them more than 4,000 children. Many are held for days without food or water in the Vélodrome d’Hiver cycling arena and then deported, most to Auschwitz. In 1995 President Jacques Chirac acknowledged the French state’s responsibility.

text.en: Wikipedia gives both 4,115 and 4,051 children among those arrested.

summary.en: From 30 October to 3 November 1911 the first Solvay Conference on Physics is held at the Hotel Metropole in Brussels. The subject is radiation and the quanta, Hendrik Lorentz chairs it, and the participants include Albert Einstein, Marie Curie, Max Planck, Ernest Rutherford and Henri Poincaré. The conferences continue today.

On 22 April 1915 the German army releases more than 170 tonnes of chlorine gas along a 6.5 km front north of Ypres. It is Germany’s first mass use of poison gas on the Western Front. The French troops in the gas cloud lost 2,000–3,000 men. The poem In Flanders Fields was written during the battle.

text.en: Wikipedia says the Second Battle of Ypres began on 22 April 1915, Wikidata on 21 April. The place agrees.

summary.en: On 14 August 1920 the Olympic Games open in Antwerp, which was given them as a tribute to the Belgians after the war. Germany, Austria, Hungary, Bulgaria and the Ottoman Empire were banned. For the first time the Olympic oath was taken, doves were released for peace and the flag with the five rings was flown.

text.en: Wikipedia gives the opening on 14 August and the closing on 12 September 1920. Wikidata gives 20 April–12 September 1920, including the events held before the opening.

summary.en: The Treaty of Versailles gives Belgium the German districts of Eupen and Malmedy, with some 64,000 inhabitants. Those against had to sign open registers in January–June 1920, and only 271 of nearly 34,000 voters did so. Nine of the area’s eleven municipalities are today Belgium’s German-speaking Community.

The priest and physicist Georges Lemaître in Leuven publishes a paper in 1927 arguing that the universe is expanding, so the galaxies move away from us. It was hardly read outside Belgium, and Einstein called the physics abominable. The law is today called the Hubble–Lemaître law, and the idea led to the Big Bang.

On 10 January 1929 Hergé, Georges Remi from Brussels, begins drawing Tintin in the Land of the Soviets in Le Petit Vingtième, the children’s supplement of a Catholic and conservative newspaper. The anti-communist strip ran weekly until May 1930 and became the first album about the reporter Tintin and his dog Snowy.

On 14 May 1940, during the German invasion, the Luftwaffe bombs Rotterdam and destroys the whole historic city centre. At least 1,150 people are killed in the May bombings, 711 of them on 14 May, and 85,000 are left homeless. Germany threatens to bomb Utrecht, and the Netherlands surrenders that afternoon.

On 25 February 1941 Amsterdam goes on strike after a German raid in the Jewish quarter, in which 425 Jewish men were taken hostage. The banned Communist Party called the strike, and 300,000 joined. The Germans crushed it within two days. It was the only large strike against the persecution of Jews in occupied Europe.

In 1911 three steel companies merge to form ARBED, which starts with 21 blast furnaces. Iron ore had been found in southern Luxembourg in the 1850s, and in 1913 the country made over a million tonnes of steel. In 2002 ARBED became part of Arcelor.

On 30 August 1942 the German occupiers declare forced conscription of Luxembourgers into the German army. On 1–3 September the country answers with a general strike that paralyses administration, farming, industry and schools. The Germans execute 21 strikers and send hundreds to concentration camps.

On 13 October 1912, 60 delegates of 31 Sorbian associations found the league Domowina in Hoyerswerda. The name means homeland. It becomes the umbrella organisation of the Sorbs in Lower and Upper Lusatia. The Nazis banned it in 1937, but it reopened in 1945 and is today the recognised representative of the Sorbs.

On 12 November 1918, during the November Revolution, the new government, the Rat der Volksbeauftragten, proclaims that all elections are to be universal, equal and secret for men and women aged 20 or over. On 19 January 1919 women in Germany vote for the first time in a national election, for the National Assembly.

On 1 April 1919 the architect Walter Gropius founds the Bauhaus art school in Weimar, which combines crafts and the fine arts. The school moves to Dessau in 1925 and Berlin in 1932, and in 1933 its leaders close it under pressure from the Nazis. The Bauhaus became one of the most influential currents in modern design.

On 9–10 November 1938 the SA, the SS and civilians attack Jews throughout Nazi Germany, and the authorities do not intervene. Over 1,400 synagogues and prayer rooms are destroyed, over 7,000 Jewish businesses damaged and 30,000 Jewish men sent to concentration camps. At least 91 are murdered; counting later deaths, the dead numbered hundreds.

On 12 November 1918 the Republic of German-Austria is proclaimed from the ramp of the Parliament in Vienna, and women gain the vote; they first vote in February 1919. The Treaty of Saint-Germain in 1919 forbade union with Germany, and the country became the Republic of Austria.

On 10 October 1920 southern Carinthia, where most people spoke Slovene, votes on belonging to Austria or to the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes. 59 per cent choose Austria, probably including about half of the Carinthian Slovenes.

Under the peace treaties Hungary must cede West Hungary to Austria, and in 1921 it becomes the state of Burgenland. In 1910, 74 per cent there spoke German, 15 per cent Croatian and 9 per cent Hungarian. After a 1921 plebiscite, Sopron and its surroundings stayed Hungarian.

On 12 March 1938 German troops enter Austria without meeting resistance, and the country becomes part of Nazi Germany. The persecution of the Jews begins at once: they are driven through the streets of Vienna, and their homes and shops are plundered. By the end of 1941, 130,000 Jews had left Vienna.

text.en: English Wikipedia’s article on the Anschluss dates the annexation to 12 March 1938, when the troops entered. Wikidata gives both 12 and 13 March, and Wikipedia’s article on Freud says 13 March.

summary.en: On 8 August 1938 the Nazis open the Mauthausen camp by a granite quarry east of Linz. The prisoners were made to work as slaves in quarries and arms factories, and of some 190,000 prisoners in Mauthausen and its nearly 100 subcamps, half died. American troops liberated the camp on 5 May 1945.

From 1926 to 1973 the Pro Juventute foundation, with the support of the authorities, takes about 590 children from Yenish families and places them in foster homes and institutions, to force the travelling people to settle. It was called Kinder der Landstrasse. In 2025 the government recognised it as a crime against humanity.

After a referendum in 1938, Romansh becomes Switzerland’s fourth national language alongside German, French and Italian, at a time when the country wanted to stress its own identity before the war. The language, which descends from the Latin of the Romans, is spoken mostly in the Grisons. Since 1996 it has been official in dealings with Romansh speakers.

As Germany, Austria-Hungary and Russia collapse at the end of the First World War, the Poles take power. On 11 November 1918, the day after Józef Piłsudski arrived in Warsaw, the Regency Council gives him command of the army. The day is celebrated as Poland’s Independence Day.

text.en: Independence came step by step: the Regency Council declared Poland independent on 7 October 1918, and Piłsudski sent a telegram about the new state on 16 November. Wikidata gives 16 November as the start of the Second Polish Republic; the globe shows 11 November, the day that is celebrated.

summary.en: On 20 March 1921 Upper Silesia, with its mixed German- and Polish-speaking population, votes on belonging to Germany or Poland. Germany wins 59.4 per cent, but after three Polish uprisings the area is divided in October 1921, and Poland gets about a third of it, including most of the industrial district.

In the summer of 1942 more than a quarter of a million Jews have been taken from the Warsaw Ghetto to Treblinka and murdered. On 19 April 1943 those who remain resist with weapons when the SS moves to empty the ghetto. It is destroyed block by block until 16 May. It was the largest Jewish revolt of the Second World War.

On 1 August 1944, as the Red Army approaches, the Polish Home Army rises against the Germans in Warsaw. The Red Army halts outside the city, and after 63 days the insurgents surrender on 2 October. Between 150,000 and 200,000 civilians die, and the Germans destroy the city in retaliation.

On 18 October 1918 a declaration of independence drafted by Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk in Washington is published. On 28 October Czech politicians peacefully take over in Prague, and the day is counted as the birthday of Czechoslovakia. The Kingdom of Bohemia ceases to exist and becomes part of the new republic.

On 2 January 1921 Karel Čapek’s play R.U.R. has its world premiere in Hradec Králové, and the National Theatre in Prague stages it from 25 January. The play gives the world the word robot, which Čapek said his brother Josef had invented. It comes from the Czech robota, forced labour.

Under the Munich Agreement of 30 September 1938, to which Czechoslovakia is not invited, Germany receives the Sudetenland, home to some three million people, most of them Germans. German troops occupy the area by 10 October. Czechs living there must accept German citizenship or are expelled.

In November 1941 the fortress town of Terezín becomes a ghetto when the first Czech Jews are taken there. Some 141,000 Jews are sent to Theresienstadt, and about 33,000 die there, mostly of malnutrition and disease. More than 88,000 are deported onwards. The Red Army liberates the ghetto on 8 May 1945.

From October 1942 the camp at Lety is a camp for Roma, guarded by Czech gendarmes. At least 1,309 people are held there, and about 326 die, among them some 30 children born in the camp. More than 500 are sent to Auschwitz. In the 1970s a pig farm is built near the site; it is demolished from 2022.

From May 1945 the Germans are expelled from Czechoslovakia, first in wild and often violent expulsions, then from January 1946 under the Potsdam Agreement. About 1.3 million are taken to the American zone of Germany and about 800,000 to the Soviet zone. The Beneš decrees take away their citizenship and property.

text.en: Figures for the number of deaths differ greatly. The West German government estimated about 270,000 deaths in 1958. A joint German–Czech historians’ commission later concluded at least 15,000 and at most 30,000.

summary.en: On 2 November 1938 the foreign ministers of Germany and Italy award southern Slovakia to Hungary. Slovakia loses 10,390 km² with 854,277 inhabitants, 59 per cent of them Hungarians, and among the towns Košice. The 1947 Paris peace treaty declares the award null and void.

On 14 March 1939 parliament votes unanimously to secede from Czecho-Slovakia. The first Slovak state in history is a client state of Nazi Germany, with Jozef Tiso as president from October. On 4 April 1945 Soviet troops march into Bratislava.

On 25 March 1942 the first transport leaves Poprad for Auschwitz with 1,000 unmarried Jewish women. By 20 October almost 58,000 Jews, two-thirds of the country’s Jews, are deported. Slovakia pays Germany 500 Reichsmarks per person. Only a few hundred survive the war.

On 29 August 1944 an uprising against the Tiso regime and the German occupation begins, with Banská Bystrica as its centre. The insurgent army grows to around 60,000 soldiers but is crushed after 60 days, on 28 October. Today 29 August is a public holiday in Slovakia.

Albert Szent-Györgyi joins the University of Szeged in 1930. There he and Joseph Svirbely show that a substance he had found earlier in adrenal glands is vitamin C, and in some experiments they take it from paprika. In 1937 he receives the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

After the German occupation in March 1944, more than 434,000 Jews are deported from Hungary between 15 May and 9 July, most of them to Auschwitz. In Budapest 70,000 Jews are shut into a ghetto from 29 November until Soviet troops liberate it on 18 January 1945. More than half a million Hungarian Jews died.

text.en: The sources differ on the numbers. Two contemporary reports give 434,351 and 437,402 deportees. The historian Randolph Braham estimates just over 564,000 Hungarian Jews dead in 1941–1945; Wikipedia on Hungary gives over 600,000.

summary.en: On 19 March 1922 the first Vasaloppet starts, 90 kilometres on skis from Sälen to Mora. 119 skiers set off, and Ernst Alm of IFK Norsjö wins in 7 hours and 32 minutes. The race commemorates Gustav Vasa’s flight between Mora and Sälen from the soldiers of Christian II in the winter of 1520–1521.
